articles.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.summary: Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
articles.full_text:
Image source, VCG/VCG via Getty Images By Osmond Chia ,  Business reporter   and   Angus Thompson 
- Published 30 October 2026 
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record. 
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses". 
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach". 
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. 
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack. 
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record". 
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. 
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen. 
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added. 
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. 
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody. 
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. 
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack. 
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens. 
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs. 
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past. 
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets. 
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice." 
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue. 
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop. 
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement. 
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak." 
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete. 
In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." 
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them." 
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets. 
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said. 
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack. 
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds. 
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation. 
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue. 
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

articles.title: China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
articles.summary: His comment about Chinese leader Mao sparked anger but censorship left many wondering what exactly happened.
articles.full_text:
Image source, CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images By Fan Wang 
- Published 29 October 2026 
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media. 
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past. 
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society." 
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The Mbappé-Chairman Mao controversy explained 
China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened. 
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view. 
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment . His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport. 
Beijing later confirmed it was taking the footballer's apology "seriously". China Media Group has yet to say whether broadcasts will resume. 
But the anger online lingered. 
"An apology is the least he should do, but I don't forgive him. I support a ban on him," read a top comment on Weibo. 
Mbappé did not mention Mao by name in the interview, but many felt any joke that involved the founder of Communist China crossed a line. 
"Do you know who you hurt? He is the spiritual pillar of the Chinese people," read one Weibo comment liked by more than 700 users. 
"He's the most important figure in our history. Do you think a simple apology can make everything okay?" another wrote. 
Image source, Weibo Image caption, 
Weibo users shared the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao 
Ironically, despite the heavy backlash, many on Chinese social media are still asking what exactly the French forward said. They tried AI chatbots, which are just as censored as the Chinese internet and couldn't provide any answers. Others attempted to explain, but skirted around any mention of Mao. 
References were made to "the person on the 100 yuan note" and "the teacher", a title Mao once used for himself. Screenshots of the meme and interview were shared, with both the word "dictator" and Mbappé's face blurred out. 
Neither the Chinese foreign ministry statement nor the apologies issued by Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga mentioned Mao directly. 
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976. 
Despite the turmoil of his rule, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society, he remains a revered figure in China. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
It is illegal to "insult" or "slander" Communist Party martyrs and war heroes in China 
A portrait of Mao overlooks Beijing's Tiananmen Square, a symbol of how central he is in the modern Chinese imagination. Unlike other former Chinese leaders, his embalmed body is placed on public display there, drawing tens of thousands of visitors every day. In recent years, there has been a revival of interest in him among young people, who read his works and watch clips of him on social media. 
Chinese history books downplay the devastation during Mao's rule. The Chinese Communist Party's verdict on Mao is that his achievements outweigh his mistakes. In their eyes, he is "a great revolutionary and a great Marxist". 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Mbappe's Chinese social media Weibo account was banned from being followed by new users on Tuesday 
But outside China, history sees Mao as both a revolutionary and a dictator. And so reactions among the diaspora - dissidents as well as people whose families fled China decades ago, in the wake of Mao's rule - was very different. 
"You don't need to apologise, you are not wrong," a highly liked comment written in Chinese under the football star's X statement read. 
"The ones who should apologise are the CCP; they kidnapped the Chinese people and brainwashed them," another Chinese user wrote. 
On X and Threads, neither of which are accessible in China, the controversy spawned even more memes. Some feature Mbappé's face on other images of Mao, while others go further, placing him on the body of current Chinese leader Xi Jinping. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Dairy company Mengniu, an official sponsor of the Fifa World Cup, cut ties with the footballer after the backlash 
And then there was the rest of the internet which was simply puzzled. 
"It's honestly hard to understand... It seems like people aren't allowed to speak out against their leaders. And they expect the whole world to think the same way they do? That's ridiculous," read a top comment under Real Madrid's apology on Instagram. 
"How dare you call a dictator a dictator? Terrible," another user on X wrote.

articles.title: Hong Kong's leader apologises for deadly high-rise fire
articles.summary: The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
John Lee (centre) bowed in apology along with top officials By Tessa Wong 
- Published 29 October 2026 
The chief executive of Hong Kong, John Lee, has apologised for a massive fire that ripped through an apartment complex last year and killed 168 people. 
Speaking at a press conference, Lee promised major reforms to government departments to ensure such an incident would not happen again. 
A report by an independent committee, released by the government at the press conference, found that the fire was caused by "misconduct" by the private sector as well as "decades of failure" by government bodies. 
The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades. Dozens of people have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, fraud or corruption. 
At the start of the press conference on Thursday, John Lee said he was "deeply sorrowful" about the fire and that on behalf of his government, "I apologise to the victims as well as the city's residents". 
He then stood up and bowed, along with several top officials. 
Later he announced that the city's housing secretary Winnie Ho had resigned to take accountability for the fire. 
The independent committee's report found that the fire was most likely caused by a "glowing source, likely a cigarette" which ignited "paper materials" at the apartment complex, which was undergoing extensive renovation at the time. 
Officials have said the government may start using AI and drones with infra-red cameras to detect and identify smokers on construction sites. 
The report also found that the construction companies in charge of the renovation used sub-standard building materials and had unsafe procedures. 
This included using scaffolding nets that were not fire retardant and covering up windows with inflammable foam boards for a prolonged period of time. 
The companies had also used fake information in paperwork to "feign compliance" with regulators' rules, according to the report. 
The committee said the main contractor and consultant for the renovation, as well as several individuals associated with the project, deserved "the most severe criticisms" for the fire. 
But had the various government departments involved in the project possessed a "sense of crisis" and "paid sufficient heed" to the possibility of misconduct, it added, such behaviour as well as the fire hazards at Wang Fuk Court could have been rectified. 
The report also said there were "widespread, systematic and long-standing" practices in the construction sector that were "unlawful and dubious". There was also bid-rigging and other misconduct by various parties, including some who had connections with local mafias, it said. 
Lee said that the various government bodies involved in the case would be investigated, and that a unit in the housing bureau which conducts independent checks would be replaced. 
Lee also promised to crack down on bid-rigging, including criminalising the practice, and introduce long jail terms and heavy fines. 
Built in the 1980s, Wang Fuk Court in Hong Kong's north-eastern Tai Po district housed about 4,600 people. 
Nearly 40% of the residents were 65 or older, and many of the fire's victims were elderly people. 
Thousands of firefighters were deployed to bring the fire under control. One of them, 37-year-old Ho Wai-ho, died during the firefighting operation. 
The fire deeply shocked and worried Hong Kong, a densely populated city where many residents live in similar ageing high-rises, and sparked calls for accountability.

articles.title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.summary: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
This is the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300 By Kelly Ng   and   Ian Tang ,  BBC Monitoring 
- Published 29 October 2026 Updated 30 October 2026 
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen. 
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024. 
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering. 
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party. 
Since then, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", Zhang Fuhai, from the party's disciplinary commission, told a press briefing on Friday. 
He also said the party would enhance its efforts to ensure officials "dare not, cannot, and do not want to be corrupt". 
Anti-corruption purges continue 
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing. 
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign. 
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China. 
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption." 
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder". 
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively. 
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year. 
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members. 
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty. 
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The party says it's going after "pointless formalities", which inlcude "bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance" 
Who are the key figures purged? 
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violated [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption. 
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own". 
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote. 
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman. 
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members. 
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22. 
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged. 
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment." 
Xi's plans for the future 
Analysts believe one reason for the increased emphasis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader. 
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder of Communist China. 
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says. 
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look". 
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country. 
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says. 
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Sanrio says it will strengthen review processes for future collaborations By Koh Ewe 
- Published 29 October 2026 
Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China. 
Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative. 
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show. 
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values". 
"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday. 
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects." 
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm. 
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan . 
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas . 
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays. 
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing". 
Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer." 
When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hello Kitty has been criticised on Chinese state media and Chinese social media 
Hello Kitty is not the only internationally beloved figure to have faced such wrath in China in recent days. 
Earlier this week, several Chinese brands dropped French footballer Kylian Mbappé over comments he had made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong - which he has since apologised for. 
Vivant is about a Japanese salaryman who finds himself entangled in an international web of crime and espionage. 
Its first season, which aired in 2023, was set in a fictional Central Asian country. Its second season, which premiered in July, features Chinese agents torturing a Japanese spy by cutting his fingers and stabbing his abdomen. 
Chinese state outlets, including CCTV, argued that these tactics "highly overlap" with those historically used by Japanese troops against the Chinese, and that the drama "distorts the truth". 
Masamine Ryuho, the president of Vivant's TV network TBS, said on Wednesday that the show was completely fictional and had no intentions of "disparaging any particular country".

articles.title: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
articles.summary: Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, has been stranded in the Cook Islands since 2023 and wants to return to Sri Lanka.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Supplied By Ayeshea Perera ,  Asia Digital Editor   and   Dinuk Hewawitharana ,  BBC Sinhala 
- Published 1 hour ago 
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific. 
The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged". 
Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand. 
After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa. 
Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka. 
Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed. 
As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving. 
"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears. 
"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home." 
Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children. 
Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds. 
In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka. 
She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability. 
But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined. 
That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country. 
So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made. 
It turned out to be a disastrous decision. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guest 
She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas. 
Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do". 
"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go." 
But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa. 
Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too. 
In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand. 
Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected. 
"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down. 
Image source, Supplied 
On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest. 
She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing. 
One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income. 
"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC. 
But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped. 
Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says. 
"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont. 
She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services. 
The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response. 
McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there. 
New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions. 
To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."

Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand". 
When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim. 
Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994". 
Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this". 
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter." 
But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried. 
"Her mental state is not good," her tells BBC Sinhala. 
"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."

articles.title: The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
articles.summary: Indian chef Ranji Smile opened America’s first Indian restaurant in 1901 - then became a fake prince.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel Image caption, 
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene By Dinyar Patel Historian 
- Published 31 October 2026 
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US. 
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene. 
In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name. 
"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail". 
Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe. 
Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue. 
In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah. 
Image source, Hulton Archive/Getty Images Image caption, 
A party at New York's Sherry restaurant in 1900 
Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff. 
At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback. 
Smile, a skilled showman, thrived in this environment. 
Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon". 
Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him." 
As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier , external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome. 
Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel Image caption, 
A Washington Post headline on Ranji Smile in 1907 
Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns. 
As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans. 
Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad. 
Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flair for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity. 
Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants". 
All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported. 
Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel Image caption, 
Violet Ethel Rochlitz, Smile's wife, was featured in the Salt Lake City Tribune in 1913 
"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof. 
Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country. 
In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility. 
While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him. 
Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant. 
Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel Image caption, 
The New Haven Union in 1912 ran a story on 'Mr and Mrs Ranji Smile'. 
The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear. 
Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters. 
In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo". 
Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf). 
Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island. 
Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel Image caption, 
KY Kira opened a successful Indian restaurant in New York in 1913 
Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit. 
New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America. 
That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.

articles.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
articles.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Imogen James 
- Published 31 October 2026 
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. 
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. 
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. 
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. 
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack. 
Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. 
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. 
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. 
- 
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean 
The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed. 
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible. 
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks. 
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". 
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". 
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. 
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance. 
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide. 
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

articles.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
articles.summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Jaroslav Lukiv   and   Joe Tidy ,  Cyber correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 30 October 2026 
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist . 
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. 
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit. 
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds. 
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI. 
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort. 
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar. 
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss". 
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected". 
- 
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far 
- Published 1 day ago 
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." 
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". 
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. 
In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens. 
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York. 
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%. 
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. 
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody. 
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss. 
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm. 
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry. 
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them. 
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it". 
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. 
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. 
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers. 
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime. 
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack. 
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in. 
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling. 
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

articles.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
articles.summary: If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent 
- Published 31 October 2026 
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance , the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. 
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis. 
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted. 
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied. 
Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim. 
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives. 
- 
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far 
- Published 1 day ago 
- 
Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea 
- Published 1 day ago 
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange. 
In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency. 
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities". 
The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports. 
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected 
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain. 
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022. 
In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker. 
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme. 
Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area. 
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. 
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said. 
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for. 
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper. 
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means. 
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems. 
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

It’s closer to Beijing than Washington – and residents of this Alaskan outpost are reeling from Trump’s policies
On the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at risk 
It was less than 17 hours until the start of Alaska’s lucrative Bering Sea crab season, and Oystein Lone was standing on a dock in the city of Unalaska, preparing to embark in rough conditions. 
The problem wasn’t the next day’s forecast of 60mph gusts, which would kick up white-capped swells and make crabbing, already one of the most dangerous jobs in the United States, even more hazardous. Nor was it the question of whether there’d be enough red king, tanner and snow crabs to go around – state regulators had, in fact, announced higher quotas for the season. 
What was bothering Lone, as the sun sank lower in the sky that Wednesday evening, was the question of how to make the numbers work when diesel cost more than ever , thanks to the war with Iran. 
“This is the most challenging time I’ve seen,” said Lone, who has been fishing since 1989. He had already spent $86,000 to put 12,000 gallons of the fuel in one of his two boats, but the price had climbed higher since then, and if he wanted to fill up again, he expected to spend $100,000. 
Located further west than the Hawaiian islands, Unalaska is closer to Beijing, Tokyo and Seoul than Washington DC. Most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage, which cost at least $1,600 round trip and are prone to cancellation, due to the region’s unpredictable storms and fog. 
But Unalaska is by no means a backwater. It has been the country’s most productive seafood port by volume for more than two and a half decades, and when its crab and pollock seasons are open, thousands of deckhands and processors arrive from elsewhere to work tough but well-paying jobs on boats offshore and in seafood plants crowded in the city. 
View image in fullscreen 
Oystein Lone, the captain of the Pacific Mariner. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian 
Even here, the impacts of Donald Trump’s efforts to remake the US government in his image can be felt. Since Trump returned to the White House, the library, museum, public radio station and local government have had funding they relied on disrupted or canceled altogether. Longshoremen have been tasked with loading empty containers on to ships to avoid tariffs. And the soaring price for diesel has squeezed not just the seafood industry, but all of the nearly 4,300 residents of the city, who rely on the fuel for electricity. 
“This whole town runs on diesel,” said Daneen Looby, a longtime Unalaska resident who sits on the city council and owns the Norwegian Rat Saloon. With distributors upping the fuel surcharges she pays for food and alcohol shipments, Looby is thinking of raising her menu prices. “I didn’t want to, but I kind of have to, otherwise I’m going to become a charity.” 
The midterm elections are on Tuesday, and Alaska is set to play a major role in determining if the president’s Democratic foes regain control of Congress . Alaska resoundingly backed Trump in the 2024 election, as did a majority of Unalaska voters, but Democrats believe the president’s plunging public approval ratings together with rising fuel prices have put its two-term Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, at risk of losing re-election to their nominee Mary Peltola, even as scandals rock her campaign. 
Candidates only occasionally make the trip to Unalaska, and there are just a handful of campaign signs up around town, but outrage over the direction the country has taken since Trump returned to office is prevalent. 
“I feel like we have a rogue government right now, and I don’t feel like the Republicans are doing their job,” Looby said. “I don’t understand why Congress isn’t getting more involved.” 
‘In furtherance of the president’s agenda’
The name Unalaska derives from a word in the language of the Unangax̂ people who have lived on the island for thousands of years, and roughly translates to “near the mainland” for its proximity to Alaska’s southwestern peninsula. 
Russian fur traders arrived in the middle of the 18th century, and eventually established a colony that came under American control when Washington purchased the Alaska territory in 1867. As the second world war approached, the US military built bases on the large, mountainous island of Unalaska and the smaller Amaknak island next to it, which were connected by a single bridge in the 1970s. In June 1942, Japan staged back-to-back air raids that killed dozens, and there are still concrete pillboxes and bunkers strewn all over town and on the tops of its treeless, windswept hills. 
In 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, more than 780m pounds of catch valued at nearly $225m came through its port, Dutch Harbor, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration . Pollock, a versatile white fish, is the main product, and if you’ve eaten fish sticks, imitation crab or a Filet-O-Fish sandwich at a McDonald’s in Asia or the United States, its ingredients may well have been processed on Unalaska. The different species of crab found in the Bering Sea are also offloaded here, and the travails of that work are documented every year by camera crews who embark from Dutch Harbor to film the reality series Deadliest Catch . 
View image in fullscreen 
View image in fullscreen 
Top: A king crab on display in Amelia’s restaurant. Bottom: Crab pots wait to be unloaded. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian 
As soon as he took office in 2025, Trump began signing executive orders billed as rooting out waste from the federal government, together with the efforts of Elon Musk’s now-shuttered “department of government efficiency”. Democrats and good governance groups said the campaign undermined important functions of government, and were of dubious legality . 
One of Trump’s orders , signed in March 2025, attempted to dismantle a slew of federal agencies, including the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS). The little known office is the source of a yearly grant that Unalaska’s public library receives to buy books, and librarian Karen Kresh expected $6,000 last year, only to be told the money would not be coming. 
“It had been stable and been reliable for years and years, and that was sort of a surprise to see that instability come up with that grant,” she said. 
The main repository in the United States for cultural and natural history objects from the island chain is the Museum of the Aleutians in Unalaska. When Trump arrived in office, its staff was at work cataloging a large collection of artifacts dating back to the Russians’ first contact with the Unangax̂, funded by more than $347,000 in grant money from the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH). 
At the beginning of April, the museum’s executive director, Virginia Hatfield, received a message saying the grant was being canceled because it “no longer effectuates the agency’s needs and priorities”, and that the funds would be reallocated “in a new direction in furtherance of the president’s agenda”. The cut put the project on hold, and Hatfield was forced to lay off six people. 
“It’s very heartbreaking, and it kind of truncated important work,” she said. 
Weeks later, Republicans in Congress approved legislation ending funding for public media outlets, which they have long accused of broadcasting news with a liberal bias. The decision had significant implications for Alaska, the largest state in the country which is full of small, remote communities – like Unalaska – unreachable by road, and where cellphone service can be unreliable. 
That makes radio the best way to get word out when an emergency strikes, and the same day the Senate began debating whether to cut funding, the island’s public broadcaster KUCB was putting out warning of a potential tsunami. The wave did not arrive, and the station lost half of its budget after Trump signed the bill, said Lauren Adams, the general manager. In the months that followed, KUCB, along with other public media outlets nationwide, experienced a surge in giving from outraged listeners. It was also among more than a dozen Alaska stations to receive temporary funding from the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA). 
View image in fullscreen 
View image in fullscreen 
Lauren Adams of KUCB radio pictured in Unalaska. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian 
The station now has reserves in the bank, Adams said, but no long-term solution to the question of how to stay open, with annual federal funding gone. 
“When you get just this windfall fundraising from around the United States, what’s the sustainability of that?” Adams asked. “Eventually, we’re going to run out of those reserves and things that kept us going.” 
Lost opportunities
The second Trump administration hasn’t solely been a disruptive force in Unalaska. 
Iliuliuk Family & Health Services is the city’s only clinic, and deals with everything from checkups to emergencies. Soon, they will open a pharmacy that can replace the mail-order drugs most residents rely on, thanks to more than $400,000 from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program. 
Created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s main domestic policy legislation , the program was conceived to address concerns from Republicans that cuts to the Medicaid health insurance program for poor and disabled Americans included elsewhere in the legislation would put rural hospitals out of business. 
Most of the Medicaid provisions have not taken effect yet , but hospitals nationwide remain concerned that even with the Rural Health Transformation money, they could lose patients vital to keeping their doors open. Christy Fassbender, Iliuliuk’s chief operating officer, said that is unlikely to be an issue in Unalaska. 
“We have a very small Medicaid population. We are less than 6% for Medicare and Medicaid, and that is because this is a working town,” Fassbender said. 
Nor has the chaos the federal government experienced when Trump first began his term been permanent. In June of this year, the Museum of the Aleutians was notified that the grant from the NEH was back on, though in the time that the funding was canceled, the project director and outreach specialist Hatfield hired found other work, and the professor who had excavated the artifacts providing a glimpse into Unalaska’s past died. 
The IMLS eventually restored the funds the library uses to buy books. But recently, Kresh learned that the Federal Communications Commission was considering ending E-Rate, a program that helps the library and Unalaska’s school district provide internet access. If that were to happen, she said, the library would have to look for another way to cover the expense of offering the only free, public wifi in town, which residents and visitors rely on to apply for jobs and stay connected to the world. NEH grants that had been cut nationwide were restored after a lawsuit , and a different suit halted the closure of the IMLS. 
Unalaska has felt other consequences of Trump’s presidency, for which there appears to be little recourse. 
At Unisea, one of the largest seafood processors in the city, they’re rebuilding their workforce after shifting away from foreign guest workers, visas which have long been hard to get and eventually became too unreliable, director of Alaska operations Ron Kjorsvik said. 
View image in fullscreen 
View image in fullscreen 
Unalaska has felt the consequences of Trump’s presidency. Photograph: Brian Adams/The Guardian 
The only foreigners still doing the difficult work of processing pollock, crab, black cod and halibut are 15 Ukrainians on a special visa for nationals of the war-ravaged country, but they’ll be leaving soon – none had their visas renewed, Kjorsvik said. 
A group of congressional Democrats led by Virginia’s James Walkinshaw had complained to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) in March about delays processing such applications, and in a reply seen by the Guardian, the agency’s director said USCIS had “many competing priorities and urgent requests for consideration daily”, and could not “prioritize” Ukrainians with U4U visas. 
Seafood processing plants on the islands, meanwhile, have their own generators supplying electricity, while the rest of the city runs on a separate, generator-powered grid. Unalaska’s leaders have long contemplated alternatives, including the possibility of tapping geothermal power from a nearby volcano. 
Under Joe Biden, the Department of Energy (DOE) established the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, and Unalaska’s utility director, Erik Hernandez, said the city was in the process of applying for funds to install five one-megawatt wind turbines and a battery system on a windy parcel of land, which could have replaced most of their diesel generators. But after Trump took office, the DOE stopped communicating about the grant, and in June 2025, the city was informed the money was no longer available. 
The DOE did not respond to a request for comment. Earlier this year, the US Government Accountability Office found that the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations had lost 85% of its staff over the first six month’s of Trump’s second term, and placed a stop work order on all contracts. 
The city was as reliant on diesel as ever when the Iran war began and crude oil prices rose in tandem, and the fluctuating rate that Unalaska charges power users to cover the cost of fuel has climbed almost two thirds, from $0.22 per kilowatt hour last year, to as much as $0.36 now, Hernandez said. 
The fuel price increase has furthered the stress on a fishing industry that was already not having a great year. Pollock in 2026 have been small and scarce, and storms have been frequent. That has meant less work for Dutch Harbor’s longshoremen who move refrigerated shipping containers filled with seafood onto ships bound for Asia or the US west coast. Shawn Schomer, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s shop steward at Matson, one of the major shipping lines serving the port, said he’s recently been getting a new and unusual request from his superiors. 
Certain shipping containers that remain for too long in the United States are considered imports, and thus subject to the tariffs Trump has slapped on trading partners globally. 
“We got to get these tariff cans out of here. That’s what the management tells us,” when it asks for the containers to be loaded on outgoing vessels, Schomer said.

Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts 
Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities. 
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals. 
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.” 
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood. 
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues. 
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview. 
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression. 
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment. 
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.” 
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China. 
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said. 
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment. 
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024. 
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping 
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping. 
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year. 
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history. Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders 
Read more 
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained. 
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X. 
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty. 
View image in fullscreen 
Zhang Shengming, top, sits behind Chinese leader Xi Jinping during the opening session of the fifth plenum in Beijing. Photograph: Andy Wong/AP 
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”. 
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin. 
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body. 
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader. 
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China 
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times. 
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources. China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario 
Read more 
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development. 
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times. 
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
